key_terms.meaning: Two matched transistors sharing one tail current, with the two inputs at their bases (or gates); it responds to the difference of the inputs.
The constant current I_TAIL forced into the joined emitters (or sources) of the pair; it sets the bias and the maximum output current.
g_m = I_C/V_T = 2I_D/(V_GS − V_TH); the change in collector (drain) current per volt of input change. V_T ≈ 26 mV at room temperature.
v_id = v₁ − v₂, the part of the input the amplifier is meant to multiply.
v_icm = (v₁ + v₂)/2, the part of the input the amplifier should reject.
CMRR = |A_d/A_cm|, usually given as 20 log₁₀|A_d/A_cm| in dB; high CMRR means good rejection of the common signal.
A transistor biased by a reference current, whose geometry ratio copies that current into another branch.
The current forced into the diode-connected input side of a mirror; it defines the current that is copied.

key_terms.term: Output resistance r_o of a source
key_terms.meaning: r_o = V_A/I_C (BJT) or 1/(λI_D) (MOSFET); a larger r_o means the copied current changes less when the output voltage changes.
A current source or current mirror used in place of a load resistor, giving a small DC drop but a very large small-signal resistance.
A mirror load adds the two branch currents at one node, so one output carries the full differential signal.
A stage (emitter follower, diode stack, or current-mirror shift) that moves a DC level down without changing the signal gain.
A unity-gain stage (usually a class-AB push-pull pair) that supplies load current and gives a low output resistance.
The differential DC input needed at the terminals to make the output zero; it comes from mismatch in the input pair and load.
The small DC current flowing into (or out of) each input terminal of a real op-amp; the mismatch between the two is the input offset current.
SR = dV_out/dt maximum = I_TAIL/C_C; the fastest the output can move, set by the current available to charge the compensation capacitor.
Power-supply rejection ratio = ΔV_supply/ΔV_OS (or A_d/A_supply), usually in dB; it says how much supply ripple reaches the output.
A capacitor C_C connected across the high-gain stage, using the Miller effect to create a dominant low-frequency pole.
Miller compensation pushes the dominant pole down and the second pole up, so the amplifier stays stable in feedback.
Operational transconductance amplifier: a voltage-controlled current source with I_out = G_m(v₁ − v₂) and G_m set by an external bias current.

takeaways: A matched pair fed by one tail current sends more current down whichever side has the higher input, so it amplifies the difference and largely ignores what both inputs do together.
Any two inputs can be written as a differential part plus a common-mode part; CMRR is the single number that says how well an amplifier multiplies the first and drops the second.
A current mirror copies a reference current using geometry ratio, and its accuracy at the output is limited by the finite output resistance of the copying transistor.
Replacing load resistors with a current-mirror active load raises output resistance, increases gain, and turns a differential input into a single-ended output in one step.
An op-amp is four functions in a chain: differential input stage, high-gain stage, level shifter and output buffer.
Offset voltage and bias current are the DC errors of a real op-amp; slew rate and PSRR describe how it behaves when the signal is fast or the supply is noisy.
Miller compensation splits the two poles of a two-stage op-amp to buy phase margin, and the price is lower bandwidth and a slew rate fixed by I_TAIL/C_C.
An OTA gives an output current proportional to input voltage, with transconductance set by a bias current, which makes it easy to tune and to use in filters.
bank_note: Long answers here are usually built around drawing the circuit, writing the small-signal half-circuit, and then computing gain, CMRR, poles or slew rate from named device parameters.

bank.q: Draw a BJT differential pair with a tail current source. Explain how the tail current is steered between the two sides as the differential input changes, and what happens when both inputs move together.
outline: Circuit drawn with matched Q1, Q2, emitters joined, tail source I_TAIL
v_id = 0: current splits equally, I_TAIL/2 each side
v_id positive: Q1 takes more current, Q2 less; difference in collector currents is g_m v_id for small v_id
Full switching when |v_id| exceeds about 4V_T (≈100 mV); I_TAIL limits the maximum
Common-mode input moves both emitters together and changes almost nothing if the tail source is ideal

bank.q: Define differential-mode gain, common-mode gain and CMRR. Show how CMRR is expressed in decibels and explain why an ideal amplifier has infinite CMRR.
outline: A_d = v_out/v_id, A_cm = v_out/v_icm
v_id = v₁ − v₂, v_icm = (v₁ + v₂)/2
CMRR = |A_d/A_cm|; CMRR(dB) = 20 log₁₀|A_d/A_cm|
Ideal: A_cm = 0 so CMRR is infinite
CMRR falls when the pair or its load is mismatched

bank.q: Explain the working of a simple two-transistor current mirror. Why does finite output resistance limit how well the current is copied?
outline: Diode-connected Q1 carries I_REF, sets V_BE
Q2 has the same V_BE, so it carries the same current if matched
Geometry ratio (W/L or emitter area) sets the copy ratio
I_OUT = I_REF·(ratio) only if V_DS (or V_CE) of both devices is equal
Finite r_o gives I_OUT = I_REF·ratio·(1 + λV_DS); output current varies with output voltage

bank.q: List the four internal stages of an op-amp and state the job of each, with a typical circuit for each stage.
outline: Input stage: differential pair, provides most of the gain and CMRR, sets offset and noise
Gain stage: common-emitter or common-source, adds voltage gain
Level shifter: emitter follower or current-mirror level shift, moves DC level down to zero without losing gain
Output buffer: class-AB push-pull, low output resistance, supplies load current, often with short-circuit protection

bank.q: A BJT differential pair has I_TAIL = 1 mA, β = 100, V_A = 100 V, and collector resistors R_C = 10 kΩ. Find g_m, r_π, r_o, the differential gain and the common-mode gain.
outline: I_C = 0.5 mA per side
g_m = I_C/V_T = 0.5 mA/26 mV ≈ 19.2 mS
r_π = β/g_m ≈ 5.2 kΩ
A_d = −g_m R_C (or −g_m(R_C ∥ r_o)) ≈ −192
A_cm ≈ −R_C/(2R_EE) for a finite tail resistance; ideally 0

bank.q: A reference current of 200 µA feeds a current mirror. Design the geometry ratio to copy 100 µA, and find the change in copied current when the output voltage rises by 2 V (V_A = 50 V).
outline: Ratio = 100/200 = 0.5, so W/L of the copy is half the reference device
r_o = V_A/I_OUT = 50 V/100 µA = 500 kΩ
ΔI = ΔV/r_o = 2/500 k = 4 µA, i.e. 4% error
Mention cascode to raise r_o and reduce this error

bank.q: An amplifier has A_d = 1000 and A_cm = 0.5. Find the CMRR as a ratio and in dB. If the input pair mismatch doubles A_cm, what is the new CMRR?
outline: CMRR(dB) = 20 log₁₀ 2000 ≈ 66 dB
New A_cm = 1, CMRR = 1000, i.e. ≈ 60 dB
Statement that CMRR is set by mismatch in devices and loads, not by the tail current alone

bank.q: A two-stage CMOS op-amp has g_m1 = 1 mS, g_m2 = 4 mS, C_C = 2 pF and C_L = 5 pF. Estimate the unity-gain frequency, the two poles, and comment on the phase margin.
outline: GBW ≈ g_m1/(2πC_C) ≈ 1 mS/(2π × 2 pF) ≈ 80 MHz
Dominant pole p1 ≈ GBW/A_0 where A_0 = g_m1 R1 · g_m2 R2
Second pole p2 ≈ g_m2/(2πC_L) ≈ 4 mS/(2π × 5 pF) ≈ 127 MHz
Phase margin ≈ 90° − arctan(GBW/p2) ≈ 90° − 32° ≈ 58°
Statement that p2 must sit well above GBW, typically 2–3 times

bank.q: An OTA has G_m = 1 mS set by a bias current, driving a 10 pF load. Find the output voltage for v_id = 50 mV and the maximum rate at which the output can change if the bias current limits it to 100 µA.
outline: I_out = G_m v_id = 1 mS × 50 mV = 50 µA
V_out = I_out/(sC); for a step, the slope is I/C
Slew limit = I_bias/C_L = 100 µA/10 pF = 10 V/µs
Note that G_m itself is proportional to √I_bias (strong inversion) or I_bias (weak inversion)

bank.q: A two-stage op-amp has a tail current of 20 µA and a Miller capacitor C_C = 2 pF. Find its slew rate. What happens to slew rate and to g_m1 if the tail current is doubled?
outline: SR = I_TAIL/C_C = 20 µA/2 pF = 10 V/µs
Doubling I_TAIL doubles SR to 20 V/µs
g_m1 rises only as √I_TAIL in strong inversion, i.e. by 1.41
So GBW rises by 1.41 while SR doubles; the ratio SR/GBW improves

bank.q: Compare a resistive load with a current-mirror active load in a differential amplifier, covering gain, output resistance, voltage headroom, and how a single-ended output is obtained.
outline: Gain with resistors: A_d = −g_m R_C; with active load: A_d = −g_m(r_on ∥ r_op), much larger
Output resistance rises from R_C to r_o of two devices in parallel
Headroom is lost: the mirror needs about V_OV of drop; resistors allow rail-to-rail swing depending on bias
Mirror adds the two branch currents at one node, giving a single-ended output without a separate differential-to-single-ended stage
Common-mode gain also rises, so CMRR must be checked

bank.q: Explain Miller compensation and pole splitting in a two-stage CMOS op-amp. Discuss the trade-off between phase margin, bandwidth and slew rate.
outline: C_C placed between the input and output of the second (high-gain) stage
Miller effect multiplies C_C by (1 + A2), creating a dominant pole at low frequency
The same feedback pushes the second pole up: pole splitting
Unity-gain frequency GBW = g_m1/C_C; larger C_C lowers bandwidth
Phase margin improves with a larger C_C, but slew rate SR = I_TAIL/C_C falls
Nulling resistor or cascode compensation used to move the right-half-plane zero

bank.q: An inverting amplifier is built with an op-amp having V_OS = 5 mV and I_B = 500 nA, with a 1 MΩ feedback resistor. Analyse the output error and suggest two remedies.
outline: Output offset from V_OS = V_OS(1 + R_F/R_IN)
Bias current through R_F gives I_B R_F = 0.5 V of error — this dominates
Offset current (difference of the two bias currents) matters if both inputs see equal resistance
Remedy 1: match DC resistance at both inputs to cancel I_B effects
Remedy 2: choose a FET-input or chopper-stabilised op-amp, or add a DC trim
Conclusion: with high resistances, bias current, not offset voltage, sets the DC error

bank.q: Explain what PSRR means, why it falls with frequency, and how the internal stages of an op-amp let supply noise reach the output.
outline: Definition: change in V_OS per volt of supply change, usually in dB
DC PSRR comes from the symmetry of the input stage and the current mirrors
At high frequency, the compensation capacitor and load capacitance give a direct path from supply to output
Falls at roughly 20 dB/decade beyond the dominant pole
Bypass capacitors and supply filtering reduce the practical effect

bank.q: Explain the Gm reduction method for improving slew rate, and state the conditions under which it helps.
outline: Slew rate is limited by I_TAIL charging C_C
G_m reduction lowers g_m1 without lowering the tail current, so GBW = g_m1/C_C falls but SR = I_TAIL/C_C stays
Result: the ratio SR/GBW improves, giving more headroom before slewing
Done by source degeneration in the input pair or by lowering the input pair's W/L while keeping the same bias current
Helps when the amplifier is slew-limited rather than settling-limited; costs input-referred noise and offset

glossary.def: An amplifier whose output depends on the difference between two inputs and only weakly on their average.
The average of the two input voltages, (v₁ + v₂)/2, which an ideal differential amplifier ignores.
The difference of the two input voltages, v₁ − v₂, which the amplifier is designed to multiply.
The constant current forced into the joined emitters or sources of a differential pair; it sets bias and limits output current.
Two transistors made identically and placed close together so their parameters track over temperature and process.
The single-transistor equivalent obtained by splitting a symmetric differential circuit for differential-mode analysis.
Common-mode rejection ratio; the ratio of differential gain to common-mode gain, usually quoted in dB.
A circuit that copies a reference current into another branch, set by the ratio of device geometries.
A transistor stacked on another to raise output resistance; used to make current sources and mirrors more accurate.
The small-signal resistance seen looking into a device or source; it decides how much current changes with output voltage.
A transistor current source used as a load, giving high small-signal resistance with a small DC voltage drop.
A stage that shifts a DC voltage level without changing the signal amplitude, so the next stage is properly biased.
A unity-gain stage that drives load current and presents a low output resistance.
A pair of complementary transistors that source and sink current, usually biased in class AB.
The small differential DC voltage that must be applied to make a real op-amp's output zero.
The DC current that flows into each input terminal of a real op-amp.
The difference between the two input bias currents.
The maximum rate of change of the output voltage, usually in V/µs.
The ratio of a supply-voltage change to the equivalent input offset change it produces.
The lowest-frequency pole of an amplifier; it sets the point where gain begins to roll off.
180° minus the loop phase shift at the frequency where loop gain is unity; it measures stability in feedback.
Using a capacitor across a high-gain stage so the Miller effect creates a low-frequency dominant pole.
The effect of Miller compensation: the dominant pole moves lower and the second pole moves higher.
An amplifier whose output is a current proportional to the differential input voltage, with transconductance set by bias.
The frequency at which the open-loop gain falls to unity; for a compensated op-amp it equals the unity-gain frequency.
The frequency at which a transistor's current gain falls to unity; it links device speed to slew rate.
